name: PT NFC Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: NFC Indonesia: control without ownership, an equity with no residual
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at SELL with a Rp0 target, a full loss from the Rp1,800 price: the consolidated enterprise value does not clear the claims ranking ahead of the parent equity, the top line is a shrinking pass-through, and most of what is consolidated belongs to minorities.
thesis: The economic business is gross profit, not revenue: pass-through aggregator volume is in structural retreat, and the gross margin rises only because the low-margin volume is leaving.
Control without ownership: the group consolidates a signage subsidiary in which it holds a minority, so most consolidated net assets and losses accrue to non-controlling interests.
The balance sheet is funded by convertible notes and related-party balances, and the first half consumed cash while inventory built.
Our DCF enterprise value is smaller than the convertible notes plus the minorities book value, so the residual equity claim is zero; that floor is limited liability, not a modelling artefact.
The market capitalisation is several times the value of the group listed stake and of the controlling shareholder, and the buyback is priced above our value.

catalysts.event: Third-quarter 2026 financial statements due; first look at whether the cash burn and the inventory build continued

ESB convertible-note extension: the Altirra dollar note was pushed to 31 March 2026 at a doubled coupon and the further extension was still in process, so a further extension or a conversion decision is the live refinancing event
Buyback window closes; completion or otherwise, at a price above our value
Audited FY2026 statements; going-concern assessment and any audit modification

blocks.text: We initiate on PT NFC Indonesia Tbk at SELL with a Rp0 target, a -100.0% return from the Rp1,800 price. The target is the limited-liability floor: our discounted cash flow puts the consolidated enterprise value at 176.6bn, which is less than the convertible notes of IDR239.0bn and the book value of non-controlling interests of IDR442.4bn at 30 June 2026 [S19]. When the claims ranking ahead of the parent already exceed the whole enterprise, the residual claim on the parent equity is zero. We are not forecasting liquidation; we are saying that on our own most-probable operating path there is nothing left for the parent shareholder.

The variant view is not that the company is small or unprofitable — the market knows that. It is that the consolidated accounts flatter the parent. The group consolidates PT Digital Mediatama Maxima Tbk, in which it holds 29.3%, so the majority of the consolidated balance sheet and of the losses belongs to minorities [S18, S19]. The revenue line is almost entirely pass-through aggregator volume bought from and sold to four large customers, one of which is the controlling shareholder [S25]. Read the group as a residual claim on a thin slice of a shrinking distributor, not as a platform.

What the market pays is visible in the multiples: 26.4x forward EV/EBITDA and 4.4x price to book on a business whose return on equity is negative [S19]. The parent, PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk, is capitalised at IDR162.3bn while consolidating a subsidiary capitalised at many times that [S26, S10]. The gap is either a mispricing of the parent or of the child; our work says the child.

Three things move the value. First, gross profit retention as the low-margin volume runs off — the only line that has held. Second, cash and refinancing: the first half consumed operating cash and funded a capex step-up from bank and related-party lines [S19]. Third, minority leakage: because control rests on a minority stake, any recovery in the signage business accrues mostly to someone else. The buyback announced in November 2026 is priced above our value and would transfer value from staying holders if completed [S2, S5].

NFC Indonesia was incorporated in August 2013 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in July 2018 [S17, S25]. It describes itself as a provider of digital infrastructure for brick-and-mortar retailers: a digital product aggregator, cloud-based digital advertising, digital wholesale, content and entertainment, and, more recently, electric-vehicle infrastructure from motorcycle distribution to battery-swap stations [S17]. The company is domiciled and managed in Jakarta, with a single reportable operating structure rather than separate disclosed segments, and it employed 166.0 people at the last count [S17, S19].

The revenue mix is lopsided. In FY2025 the digital product aggregator supplied the overwhelming majority of net revenue of IDR4,070.0bn, with cloud advertising, clean-energy products and content making up the remainder; digital wholesale, which existed in FY2024, disappeared entirely [S25]. That is the business in one sentence: a pass-through distributor of other companies digital products, with a small and newer advertising and EV overlay. Gross profit, at IDR140.0bn, is the line that matters, because the aggregator revenue is bought and resold at a thin spread.

Group structure is the analytical crux. The company consolidates PT Digital Mediatama Maxima Tbk (DMMX), the cloud-advertising and digital-signage business, on a 29.3% ownership stake [S18, S19]. It also consolidates PT Energi Selalu Baru (ESB), the clean-energy and EV vehicle, on a minority stake, alongside several digital-product subsidiaries that are majority or half owned [S25]. Consolidation follows control, not ownership, so the group income statement and balance sheet include one hundred per cent of businesses the parent only partly owns. At 30 June 2026 non-controlling interests carried IDR442.4bn of book value against parent equity of IDR262.4bn — the minority is the larger claim on the consolidated net assets [S19]. Any sum-of-the-parts or earnings-based valuation that ignores this overstates the parent.

The controlling shareholder is PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk (MCAS), which holds the majority stake; a second strategic holder owns a little over a tenth, a private-bank nominee holds a single-digit block, and the remainder is public with treasury shares held by the company [S17]. Free float is 22.4% of capital, above the exchange minimum, and the stock is not on the special monitoring board [S10, S17]. The group is therefore a controlled subsidiary of a listed parent, and minority shareholders in NFCX sit behind both the parent and the non-controlling interests inside the consolidated perimeter.

Strategy has moved toward EV infrastructure and toward buying larger stakes in existing subsidiaries. The June 2025 private placement of up to 66.7 new shares was justified by raising ownership in subsidiaries and other digital businesses, with no definitive target named at the time [S12]. ESB raised pre-Series A money from SAIC Capital and LX Ventures, the LG Group vehicle, in 2024 [S13], and Volta, the group electric motorcycle brand, has since partnered with Gesits on a jointly branded model and with EcoSecurities on a carbon-credited distribution programme [S8, S7]. These are real operating initiatives, but they sit inside subsidiaries where the parent owns a minority, so their value accrues to the group and to its partners before it accrues to NFCX shareholders.

Competitively, NFCX is a challenger with no scale advantage. It does not own the demand — its largest customers are marketplaces and a convenience-retail chain — and it does not own the products, which are telco and digital vouchers sold on behalf of issuers [S25]. Its position rests on distribution reach into small retailers and on the DMMX signage estate. That is a real asset, but it is a distribution asset in a business where the counterparties have more bargaining power, which is the subject of the next section.

NFCX sits at the intersection of three Indonesian industries with very different economics: digital-product aggregation for retail, out-of-home cloud advertising, and electric two-wheelers. The first is a distribution business, the second is a media-rental business, and the third is a capital-intensive manufacturing and distribution business. The company reports one consolidated perimeter, so the reader has to separate them from the segment note rather than from the income statement [S25].

The aggregation market is large but structurally commoditised. Digital products — mobile credit, data, game vouchers, bill payments — reach consumers through marketplaces, convenience retail and thousands of small shops. NFCX intermediates between product issuers and those retail points. Its FY2025 disclosure shows how little of that chain it owns: four customers each bought more than a tenth of consolidated net revenue, led by Shopee at IDR819.6bn and including the controlling shareholder MCAS at IDR304.1bn, and together those four accounted for a disclosed share of the total that leaves the rest of the customer base fragmented [S25]. When the buyer is a marketplace with its own wallet and the supplier is a telco with its own distribution, the aggregator earns a spread that competition compresses over time. Nothing in the filings shows a contractual exclusivity, a licence or a data asset that would stop a retail chain or a marketplace from going direct.

Cloud advertising through DMMX is the better business on paper: digital signage in retail outlets, sold as a network, with recurring placement revenue. It grew in FY2025 while aggregation shrank [S25]. But it is also the business the parent only partly owns, and it competes against the large media owners and against the retail chains themselves, who can monetise their own screens. Its scale within the group is still small relative to aggregation.

Electric vehicles are the growth story management tells. ESB raised external capital from SAIC Capital and LX Ventures [S13]; Volta launched a jointly branded model with Gesits [S8] and a carbon-credited distribution programme with EcoSecurities [S7]. The strategic logic is to use the retail network as a distribution channel for two-wheelers and battery swap. The economics are not yet visible in the consolidated accounts, where clean-energy products and services remain a small revenue line [S25], and the EV business sits inside a minority-owned subsidiary. We treat it as an option that belongs mostly to the minority and to the strategic partners.

Competitive position is challenger, not leader. The aggregation market has many intermediaries and low entry barriers; the advertising network has capital barriers but strong incumbent media owners; the EV market has global manufacturers with far lower unit costs [S25, S13]. NFCX has no pricing power in any of the three. Its only durable asset is the retail footprint and the installed signage base, and neither is exclusive.

Aggregators in digital products typically earn a thin commission per transaction and depend on volume and working-capital turns; the model is closer to distribution than to software, and gross margin is the honest measure of pricing power. Out-of-home advertising earns on occupancy and audience measurement. Electric two-wheelers are a scale manufacturing business. Judged on those economics, a conglomerate spanning all three is unlikely to earn excess returns without a dominant position in one.

Regulation cuts both ways. The buyback is being executed under the financial-sector authority regulations that allow repurchases in volatile markets without a prior shareholder vote [S2]. The exchange has previously flagged unusual market activity in NFCX and its parent, which is a monitoring action and not a finding of wrongdoing, but it is a governance signal worth carrying [S14]. Electric-vehicle policy support is a swing factor for the Volta business; we cannot source the current incentive schedule from a primary document, so we do not put a value on it.

The five forces summary is unkind. Supplier power is high because product issuers set wholesale prices; buyer power is high because four customers are large and one is the parent; the threat of substitutes is high because marketplaces and retail chains can integrate backwards; new entrants face low barriers in aggregation; and rivalry is intense because the service is undifferentiated. The moat is distribution density, and it is not widening — the revenue base has shrunk every year since the peak [S25]. External influences are consumer spending on digital products, advertising budgets, the rupiah (the group carries dollar convertible notes), and Indonesian interest rates, which set the cost of the bank and related-party funding that keeps the balance sheet afloat.

The financial history is a controlled shrink. Net revenue ran at 9,836.6bn in FY2022 and 9,526.1bn in FY2023, fell to 6,074.3bn in FY2024 and 4,070.0bn in FY2025, and the first half of 2026 came in at IDR1,229.6bn against IDR2,135.5bn a year earlier [S24, S25, S19]. Gross profit did not follow revenue down: it was 124.7bn in FY2022, 136.8bn in FY2023, 130.5bn in FY2024 and IDR140.0bn in FY2025, and the gross margin has climbed from 1.4% to 3.4% as the low-margin volume left [S24, S25]. That is the one genuine positive in the story: management has been willing to give up revenue it did not earn a spread on. The corollary is that the remaining revenue base is much smaller and the fixed cost base did not shrink as fast.

Operating expenses were 98.7bn in FY2022, 141.8bn in FY2024 and IDR131.5bn in FY2025, and first-half 2026 ran at roughly half the FY2025 level on an annualised basis [S24, S25, S19]. The operating result is now carried on the filing's own operating-profit line for both years, 8.5bn in FY2025 and -11.2bn in FY2024, because the data pack's figure was struck on its understated cost base; at those numbers the business is a rounding error at the operating line and loses money below it [S25]. Depreciation is the item the data pack gets wrong: the consolidated statements charge IDR73.5bn in FY2025 and IDR80.6bn in FY2024, because the signage and content-management fleet is depreciated through cost of revenue, and we restate history on those figures rather than on the fraction the pack carries [S25]. EBITDA on the restated basis is 82.0bn, not the number a screen would show.

The bottom line is dominated by non-operating items. FY2023 carried a -486.6bn non-operating charge and FY2024 a -129.9bn charge, which is why reported net losses of -477.8bn and -147.1bn dwarf the operating result; both look like impairments of the digital-asset and subsidiary portfolio rather than cash costs [S24, S25]. FY2025 reported a small parent profit of 5.6bn, helped by unrealised investment gains. We treat these as non-recurring and forecast them at zero; the operating business is what we value.

The first half of 2026 is the current reality. Revenue of IDR1,229.6bn produced gross profit of IDR56.2bn, a net loss of IDR50.8bn and a parent loss of IDR21.5bn [S19]. Operations consumed IDR49.4bn of cash, capex absorbed IDR80.1bn, and the cash balance ended at IDR108.7bn [S19]. The working-capital flag is inventory, not receivables. Inventory rose from IDR216.0bn at the end of FY2025 to IDR314.0bn, a build of nearly half in six months while revenue fell: either the group is stocking hardware it cannot sell quickly, or it is financing its customers. Trade receivables did the opposite — third-party receivables fell to IDR164.2bn and related-party receivables were IDR10.5bn — so we withdraw the previous draft's claim that receivables rose by roughly half, which the filing contradicts [S19]. Inventory of IDR314.0bn is more than twice the FY2026E gross profit of IDR112.4bn, which is what makes it the flag that matters.

The balance sheet is where the equity argument is settled. At 30 June 2026 parent equity was IDR262.4bn and non-controlling interests IDR442.4bn, so the minority owns the larger share of consolidated book value [S19]. The group carried IDR239.0bn of dollar convertible notes, IDR84.3bn of long-term bank loans, IDR5.0bn of financing payables and IDR14.3bn of lease liabilities — the debt-like instruments, which together are just under half of the IDR691.9bn that the financial-instruments note labels total financial liabilities. The rest of that category is trade payables, other payables, accrued expenses, customer deposits and taxes payable: operating balances, not debt. The previous draft read that whole category as leverage, overstating the liability stack roughly twofold; the risk section below is restated on the four debt-like lines, and the valuation retires the same set net of cash [S19]. Cash of IDR108.7bn against it is thin, and the first-half cash flow shows why: the operating and investing outflow was funded by drawing bank and related-party lines rather than by the business.

Our forecast holds the second half of 2026 near the first-half run-rate, then fades the decline: revenue of 2,459.1bn in FY2026E and 2,090.2bn in FY2027E, gross margin of 4.6% rising to the low single digits and held there, operating expenses near the current absolute level, and EBITDA of 63.9bn and 59.8bn [S19, S25]. Parent net loss stays small, at -11.7bn and -9.3bn, because most of the loss is absorbed by minorities. Capex is 152.7bn: we carry the first half's IDR80.1bn at roughly twice its rate on the smaller revenue base, because no second-half capital plan is disclosed that would justify a step-down, and the previous draft's assumption that spending halved in the second half was unsourced optimism rather than conservatism [S19]. Working capital releases as revenue shrinks, which is the only reason the forecast shows free cash flow at all.

Cash now sits on one basis through history and forecast. The LK reports FY2025 cash of IDR145.8bn and FY2026E is 190.4bn on the same basis, with the other-investments line kept separate instead of being bundled into cash as the data pack does; the forecast year-end position is therefore net debt of 53.9bn, not the net cash the previous draft claimed [S25, S19]. Two limits on the table have to be stated. The model debt line of 244.4bn is the pack's interest-bearing line — convertibles, financing and leases — and excludes the IDR84.3bn of bank loans that the filing includes in debt-like instruments, because net borrowing is held at zero. And the cash build depends on releasing working capital from a shrinking business, a one-off source that cannot repeat once the revenue base stabilises. Neither flatters the valuation, which uses the filing's full debt-like stack rather than the model's narrower line.

Tax needs its own paragraph. The model books no tax in any forecast year because the engine charges the statutory rate only on positive consolidated pre-tax profit, and our pre-tax line is negative. The group nonetheless paid IDR27.7bn of cash tax in the first half of 2026 against a pre-tax loss, because profitable subsidiaries cannot offset loss-making ones [S19], and the prior-year half was a fraction of that. The engine cannot express a group cash tax when the consolidated result is a loss, so rather than leave the outflow out we deduct its present value as a claim in the valuation bridge at the annualised first-half rate. The cash-tax claim is larger than the investment assets we credit, so it makes the residual worse, not better.

Capital allocation has been defensive for years. No dividend has been paid since listing, and the company has instead bought back and re-sold treasury shares and attempted new equity through private placement [S12, S15, S19]. On the two years whose depreciation we restate from the notes, capex of 41.3bn and 45.8bn ran at between half and two-thirds of the 80.6bn and 73.5bn charge, so the group has been consuming its asset base rather than growing it — the opposite of the growth-spending reading, and consistent with a distributor in retreat [S25, S19]. We withdraw the earlier claim that capex exceeded depreciation in each of the last three years: it was true only of FY2023, and only because that year still carries the data pack's un-restated depreciation. The consequence is that the FY2026E step-up to 152.7bn is a break with the last two years and rests entirely on the first-half evidence rather than on a pattern. The November 2026 buyback of up to 49.0mn shares at an estimated Rp1,775 per share, a total near IDR87.0bn, would consume most of the IDR108.7bn of cash on hand if completed, and it is priced far above our value [S2, S5].

Earnings-quality flags, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is not the problem: the losses are cash losses, not accounting losses, because the impairments were taken in earlier years and the current shortfall is operating cash burn. The divergence flag is inventory, which grew by nearly half against a falling revenue line and is optics-class until explained; receivables do not show the same pattern and we withdraw that claim. Related-party flows are large — IDR304.1bn of revenue from the controlling shareholder, plus related-party payables and receivables on the balance sheet [S25, S19]. The structure flags are the consolidated minority stake in DMMX, which is legal and disclosed but concentrates value outside the parent, and a buyback funded from retained earnings while the group carries an accumulated deficit [S19, S2]. We found no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue; this is a governance-and-structure problem, not a manipulation call.

We value NFCX on a discounted cash flow to the firm, weighted one hundred per cent, because the alternatives do not survive contact with the accounts. A multiples approach needs a comparable set of profitable distributors or ad networks; NFCX is loss-making at the parent, its EBITDA is a small residual after a depreciation charge that the data pack understates, and its return on equity is negative, so earnings multiples are undefined or meaningless [S19, S25]. A price-to-book approach on the 4.4x multiple the market pays would value a business with negative returns as if it earned its cost of capital. The DCF at least forces the operating economics and the capital claims into one frame, which is exactly what this name needs.

The cost of equity is 15.7%: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, and a levered beta of 1.47. The after-tax cost of debt is built from a pre-tax 9.4% and the statutory tax rate, and the weights are 77.7% equity and 22.3% debt. The resulting WACC of 13.8% sits above the house IDR band, and we accept that we have to argue it rather than assume it. We do: the equity is a micro-cap with a thin free float of 22.4%, a controlling shareholder, and a balance sheet that depends on related-party funding; a beta near one and a half reflects a stock that has fallen from a much higher price and trades in a narrow, illiquid market. A higher discount rate lowers the enterprise value, so the reader should know that this is not where the rating comes from — the sensitivity grid below shows the value per share at zero across the entire tested range of discount rates and terminal growth.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR176.6bn. Before defending the number we should say what it is made of, because the previous draft's "terminal value is only a fifth" line misdescribed it. FY2026E free cash flow is IDR64.8bn, and it is positive only because working capital releases IDR-151.9bn; before that release operations and capex consume cash, and the same is true in smaller amounts through FY2030E. The discounted FY2026 year contributes roughly a fifth of the enterprise value, all of it the liquidation of working capital, largely the inventory build reversing; excluding that year entirely the enterprise value falls by about that fifth. So this is not a terminal-value artefact — terminal value is 22.3% — but it is not an operating cash flow either: it is a recovering balance sheet with a small operating stub behind it. That matters for the downside, not for the sign of the answer. On whether the IDR314.0bn of inventory converts at book, we assume it does and it still leaves no residual.

The EV/sales leg that the industry template weights is the cross-check the red team asked for, and we run it as a test rather than a weighted value. The peer median is a fraction of a turn of sales, but those peers earn platform gross margins of a different order; NFCX earns 4.6% on pass-through volume, so the same multiple would imply roughly fifteen times gross profit and a positive equity value only by importing a different business. Our own DCF implies less than a tenth of a turn of FY2026E revenue, the claims are cleared only at about three-tenths of a turn, and the price implies about half a turn. The multiple is disclosed and bounded, but at a pass-through-appropriate level it is not a separate opinion on value; weighting it at the peer median would put the target near the market price on an assumption the gross margin refutes [S19, S25]. That is why the weights differ from the template default, and why the difference is recorded as a justified exception.

We then bridge to equity the only way the structure allows, and we credit every non-operating asset the balance sheet carries [S19]. The enterprise value must retire the debt-like stack net of cash and then satisfy the IDR442.4bn book value of non-controlling interests, and it is credited with IDR101.5bn of associates, IDR62.5bn of investment in shares, IDR40.0bn of convertible bonds and IDR31.5bn of other investments — the last three were omitted from the previous bridge and add about as much as the DMMX stake is worth at market. It is also debited with the capitalised structural cash tax described in the financial section. On that full arithmetic the equity value is negative and the parent claim floors at zero. We state the distance plainly rather than leave it in a table: the enterprise value would have to rise to roughly four times what our DCF produces before the parent retains anything, the breakeven is about three-tenths of a turn of FY2026E revenue, and before the limited-liability floor the parent equity value is negative by a little under half the current share price per share. The claims are therefore not close to the enterprise value, so the answer does not hinge on the last hundred billion of assets.

The market-based sum of the parts is the strongest argument against us, and we now do its arithmetic rather than dismiss it. DMMX is capitalised at IDR946.2bn; the 29.3% stake is therefore a fraction of that, and the minority's remaining holding, marked at the same price, is worth considerably more than the parent's stake. That is the point: if the asset is marked to market the claim on it must be too, and the minority at market is about half again its book value, which widens the gap rather than closing it. The per-share result is stark and we print it: DMMX at IDR946.2bn against a 29.3% stake makes the parent's holding worth a little under a quarter of NFCX's own market capitalisation, and therefore a little under a quarter of the Rp1,800 price per share, before any deduction for the operating businesses that lose money. Because the share count is the same on both sides, that fraction of the capitalisation is also the per-share fraction. The stake at market is in fact smaller than the book value of the minorities consolidated beside it, which is why marking the child to market does not create value for the parent. A sum of the parts that values the aggregator, EV and content businesses at zero still leaves a small fraction of the price; one that values them at what our DCF implies for the consolidated group leaves nothing, because the group enterprise value is below the market value of DMMX alone. Marking the stake at market therefore does not rescue the equity; it tells us the only liquid marker in the structure is a subsidiary a buyer can own directly [S21, S19].

The second cross-check is the parent. MCAS, which controls and consolidates NFCX, is capitalised at IDR162.3bn while NFCX itself is capitalised at a multiple of that [S26, S10]. Either the market values the child far above what its own controlling shareholder is worth, or the parent is depressed. Both readings are bearish for NFCX: in the first, the child is the mispriced leg; in the second, the control block is worth less than the price implies.

The sensitivity table is uninformative in a way that is itself the finding: every cell is zero. Across one percentage point either side of the discount rate and terminal growth, and across four points either side of revenue growth and two points of gross margin, no combination clears the claims ranking ahead of the parent. We flag this as the weakest link in the work, because a valuation that cannot move is a valuation the reader should test rather than accept. The test we would apply is the one the red team will: mark the minority at market, add back the DMMX stake, and see whether a residual survives the related-party and bank liabilities. On the disclosure available, it does not.

What the price implies is therefore not a growth rate we can solve for. The reverse DCF does not return a solution — the current price is not bracketed by the tested range of the revenue driver, which means the market is paying for something other than the cash flows: a control event, a recapitalisation, or the option value of the EV business. We cannot source any of those. The 26.4x forward EV/EBITDA the price implies is a multiple for a growing, asset-light platform, applied to a shrinking distributor with negative parent earnings [S19]. The multiple-survival test fails on the way in and on the way out.
The risks that matter here are balance-sheet risks, not demand risks. We rank them by likelihood and impact, and the first one dominates.

Liquidity and refinancing is the highest-likelihood, highest-impact risk, and its size depends on which line you read. The group ended the first half with IDR108.7bn of cash. The financial-instruments note reports IDR691.9bn of liabilities at amortised cost, but that category also carries trade, other and related-party payables, accrued expenses, customer deposits and taxes payable; the debt-like part is IDR239.0bn of dollar convertible notes, IDR84.3bn of long-term bank loans, IDR5.0bn of financing payables and IDR14.3bn of lease liabilities — roughly half the reported category and still more than twice the cash on hand, which is the framing we work from [S19]. The convertible stack is where the clock runs. Its largest component is a dollar note ESB issued to Altirra International Ventures in March 2023 with a principal of 5.0m dollars, a six per cent coupon and a two-year term; in February 2026 the parties extended maturity to 31 March 2026 and doubled the coupon to 12.0%, and the further extension letter ESB filed on that date was still in process at the reporting date [S19]. A note that must be re-papered every few months at a doubled coupon is the one concrete refinancing event in these accounts, and it is dollar-denominated, so a weaker rupiah raises it in rupiah terms; our macro desk already carries a rupiah path weaker than spot. If the note and the bank lines are not renewed on similar terms, the group sells assets, raises equity below our value, or leans further on the parent. Any of those is dilutive or value-destructive for the minority.

Customer concentration is the highest-impact operating risk. Four customers each bought more than a tenth of net revenue in FY2025, the largest at IDR819.6bn, and one of them is the controlling shareholder at IDR304.1bn [S25]. Losing a marketplace account, or a change in commercial terms with the parent, removes a large block of revenue with little notice. The aggregator has no contractual lock-in that we can source.

Related-party dependence is a governance and liquidity risk at once. The group sells to MCAS and funds itself from related-party balances; the terms of those balances are disclosed but not negotiated at arm length in any sense a minority can test [S25, S19]. If the parent needs cash, the direction of flow can reverse quickly.

Execution risk in electric vehicles is high-likelihood, medium-impact. The Volta and ESB initiatives are real [S13, S8, S7], but they sit in a minority-owned subsidiary, they compete with global manufacturers on cost, and the consolidated clean-energy revenue line is still small [S25]. We give the option no value in the base case; the risk is that capital continues to flow into it ahead of returns.

Currency, regulatory and structure risks are secondary but additive. The dollar convertibles transmit rupiah weakness into the equity [S19]. The exchange has previously flagged unusual market activity in the stock and its parent [S14]; that is not a violation, but it is a monitoring status that can recur. The buyback, funded from retained earnings while the group carries an accumulated deficit, transfers value from staying holders if executed at the disclosed price [S2, S19].

The scenarios mirror the same two drivers: revenue growth eight points a year either side of base and gross margin one point either side. We weight the base case most heavily, with the bear slightly larger than the bull because the customer and funding risks are asymmetric to the downside. The uncomfortable result is that all three scenarios produce a zero value per share, because even the bull operating path does not generate enough enterprise value to clear the debt-like claims and the minority at book. We state that plainly rather than dress the table up: the scenario values are not a distribution of target prices, they are all the same floor, and the useful information is in the operating paths behind them. The red team should test whether the bull case deserves a positive residual; if it does, the target is a few tens of rupiah rather than zero, which is still a fraction of the current price. The rating does not turn on that distinction.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. Two consecutive quarters of stable gross profit with positive operating cash flow would tell us the shrink has stopped. A reduction in related-party balances funded from operations, rather than from new related-party lending, would tell us the balance sheet is self-sustaining. A credible recapitalisation that converts the notes into equity at a price that leaves a residual, or a tender offer for the minorities at a premium, would change the arithmetic entirely. Conversely, a missed coupon, a qualified audit opinion, or a further equity issue at a discount would confirm the path we describe. We would also revisit if the company disclosed a binding plan to simplify the group structure by buying in the DMMX minority, because that is the one transaction that could transfer value to the parent rather than away from it.

Ownership is concentrated and layered. PT M Cash Integrasi Tbk holds the controlling stake, a second strategic holder owns a little over a tenth, a private-bank nominee holds a single-digit block, and treasury shares are held by the company; the public holds the remainder [S17]. The share registrar reports the public at 30.2% of capital and treasury at a fraction of one per cent as of August 2026; the data provider's 22.4% is a narrower float convention that strips the nominee and insider blocks, and we quote the registrar figure as primary [S17, S10]. The stock is not on the special monitoring board, it is not a konglo name in the house registry, and no index deletion or enforcement action is recorded [S3, S4]. The control structure is nonetheless the governance issue: a listed company controlled by another listed company, which is itself controlled by a family group, with minorities at the bottom of the chain.

Related-party dealing is material and runs in both directions. The controlling shareholder was one of the four customers above a tenth of net revenue in FY2025, at IDR304.1bn [S25]. The group also carries related-party payables and receivables and a long-term related-party balance, all disclosed with terms [S19]. On any reading, the parent is simultaneously the controlling shareholder, a customer, and a lender. That is legal and disclosed, but it means the minority cannot rely on arm-length pricing, and it weakens the case for any valuation that treats consolidated revenue as if it were earned on market terms.

We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the documents reviewed, no auditor modification in the archived copy we could read, and no litigation disclosure of consequence; we state that as a limit of the review rather than as a clean bill of health, because the audit report pages were not extractable from the archived text and we could not verify the opinion or any emphasis-of-matter paragraph. This is an open item for the next update and the red team should treat it as such. Management asserts a going-concern basis with no material uncertainty in the FY2025 statements [S25]; our own reading of the first-half cash flow is that the assertion depends on continued related-party and bank support rather than on operating cash generation.

The buyback is the governance question the red team put best, and we take it head-on. Up to 49.0mn shares at Rp1,775 is IDR87.0bn against IDR108.7bn of group cash while our model says the equity is worth zero: either the board sees something the accounts do not, or the programme is not a value signal at all. The file supports the second reading without fully proving it. The company's previous buyback left it holding treasury shares that it then announced it would re-sell in full — a fixed number of shares transferred through a broker over a five-month window starting in November 2025 — which is the behaviour of a treasury trading operation rather than of an insider buying value [S15]. The new programme is an order of magnitude larger and cannot be a trading operation at this liquidity: 49.0mn shares against a daily turnover of IDR54.0m would take years to execute. So the signal is ambiguous and we say so: we do not treat the board's price as information we can verify, and a buyback above intrinsic value transfers wealth from stayers to sellers whatever the motive [S2, S5, S15].

The June 2025 placement is worth stating precisely, because the previous draft overstated it. The plan was to issue 66.7mn new shares — a tenth of capital — at a nominal value of Rp100 per share; the archived article gives no issue price and names no subscriber, and the share count at 31 December 2025 shows the placement did not proceed [S12, S25]. We therefore do not claim a placement discount and cannot identify the subscriber. The governance point survives in weaker form: a company that has repeatedly sought discounted equity and re-sold treasury shares has a record of issuing at prices below the market, and no terms are disclosed on which any future issue would be struck [S12, S15].

The dividend record is empty: no dividend has been paid since the listing, and the company has instead re-sold treasury shares and attempted new equity [S15, S12, S10]. The November 2026 buyback is the first return of capital in any form, and it is being funded from retained earnings at a price above our value, which is a transfer from continuing holders to sellers [S2, S5]. We would rather see the cash retained against the notes.

ESG exposure is mostly the EV story. The group markets electric motorcycles and a battery-swap network as an emissions-reduction business, and has partnered on a carbon-credited distribution programme [S7, S8]. That is a genuine transition exposure if the business scales, but it is not measurable in the consolidated accounts and it sits in a minority-owned subsidiary. We could not source a sustainability report with quantified targets, so we do not credit any ESG premium. Governance, not environmental factors, is the ESG risk that matters here: control, related-party terms, and the minority structure.

The dated catalysts are the reporting calendar and the buyback window. The third-quarter 2026 statements are due at the end of November 2026 and are the first test of whether the first-half cash burn and inventory build continued [S9]. The buyback runs to 8 February 2027 at an estimated Rp1,775 per share [S2]; completion at that price is value-negative for holders who stay, and non-completion tells us the company could not or would not spend the cash. The audited FY2026 statements, due by the end of March 2027, will carry the going-concern assessment and any audit modification [S9]; that is the event that could re-rate the credit risk in either direction. Any announcement on the convertible notes or on a group simplification is a live catalyst we would act on immediately: the note maturing 31 March 2026 carried a twelve per cent coupon after the February amendment and the extension letter filed on the maturity date was still in process, so the next extension or a conversion is the event that decides whether the debt-like stack grows or turns into equity [S19].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are gross profit and gross margin, operating cash flow, the cash balance against the convertible notes and bank lines, inventory and receivables relative to revenue, the related-party balances with MCAS, and the DMMX ownership percentage; all are reported in the half-year and annual filings [S19, S25]. We also watch the buyback execution and any new share issuance [S2]. None of these requires a quarterly model rebuild; each is a direct read on whether the shrink is stabilising and whether the funding structure is holding.

bear.narrative: Volume erosion accelerates as the aggregator loses another anchor telco or distributor account, revenue falls eight points a year faster than base, and gross margin gives back a point as hardware mix does not stick. The cash burn persists, bank lines are not renewed on the same terms, and the equity is worth nothing because net debt and minorities exceed enterprise value.

bull.narrative: Smart Commerce and the Volta distribution build hold the customer base, revenue declines eight points a year slower than base and gross margin gains a point from hardware and advertising mix, so the group reaches a small operating profit by FY2028 and the depreciation-heavy asset base starts to throw off free cash that can be used against the bank lines.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: The top line is pass-through digital-product volume, not a stable annuity. FY2025 net revenue fell 33% and first-half 2026 fell 42% to Rp1,230bn as the group walked away from low-margin aggregator volume; we hold the second half at the first-half run-rate and then fade the decline as the mix shifts to hardware and Smart Commerce, ending at 2% nominal in the terminal year. Gross profit, not revenue, is the thing to watch: it was Rp140bn in FY2025 against Rp125bn in FY2022 on 59% less revenue.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Gross margin has risen every year as pass-through volume leaves: 2.0% in FY2024 (LK), 3.4% in FY2025 and 4.6% in first-half 2026. We take the first-half 2026 level for FY2026 and add twenty basis points to 5.0% from FY2027 as the higher-margin hardware, advertising and EV mix grows, holding it flat thereafter because a distributor has no pricing power to defend more.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses (including the Rp16.9bn of G&A depreciation in the LK's total) were Rp131.5bn in FY2025 and Rp64.1bn in first-half 2026, so roughly Rp128bn annualised. We cut the absolute cost base to about Rp126bn in FY2026 and Rp113bn in FY2027, which as a share of a shrinking top line rises to 5.2% and then eases as revenue stabilises. No further cost-out is assumed beyond what management has already delivered two years running.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation was Rp73.5bn in FY2025 and Rp80.6bn in FY2024, not the fraction the data pack carries, because the digital-signage and content-management fleet is depreciated through cost of revenue. We hold the charge near Rp75bn in FY2026 and let it drift down with the asset base rather than with revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: First-half 2026 alone consumed Rp80.1bn of property and equipment, more than the whole of FY2025 (Rp47.7bn of additions), as inventory and hardware for Smart Commerce were built out. There is no disclosed second-half capital plan that would justify a step-down, so FY2026 carries the first half at twice its rate (Rp160.2bn) rather than the Rp105bn the previous draft assumed; the ratio then cuts back toward the FY2024-25 norm from FY2027 as the build completes. Capex has exceeded depreciation in each of the last three years, so there is no maintenance-only case to argue.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Current assets of Rp920.3bn less current liabilities of Rp655.0bn at 30 June 2026 is Rp265bn, 8.4% of last-twelve-month revenue. Inventory alone rose to Rp314bn from Rp216bn in six months, so the ratio is higher than the 5.1% the pack carries on the FY2025 balance sheet; the shrinking top line releases working capital in the forecast, which is a real but one-off cash source.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The group paid Rp27.7bn of cash tax in first-half 2026 against a pre-tax loss, because the profitable subsidiaries cannot offset the loss-making ones. We use the 22% statutory rate on positive pre-tax profit and let the loss years carry no credit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance expenses of Rp7.4bn on opening bank and lease debt in FY2025; the dollar convertible notes at ESB carry 6-12%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp5.8bn on the FY2024 closing cash balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Held at zero. The first half needed Rp129bn of operating and investing cash outflow and funded it from bank lines and related-party balances; we assume no further facility is drawn in the base case rather than assume the group can keep borrowing at this pace.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. FY2025's reported profit was carried by a Rp28.1bn unrealised gain on other investments and first-half 2026 by a Rp19.2bn foreign-exchange loss on the dollar convertibles; neither is a recurring operating item, so neither is forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests held Rp442.4bn of the Rp704.8bn consolidated equity at 30 June 2026, and absorbed Rp29.2bn of the Rp50.8bn first-half loss. DMMX is only 29.3% owned but consolidated, so the minority share is structural; we use 55%, between the FY2025 ratio and the 58% first-half 2026 ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No dividend has been paid since the 2018 listing and unappropriated retained earnings were a Rp79.5bn deficit at end-2025, worsening to Rp101.1bn at 30 June 2026; the November 2026 buyback is explicitly funded from retained earnings, which competes with any distribution.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The 49m-share buyback runs from 9 November 2026 to 8 February 2027 and may not complete; at Rp1,775 it is above our value, so completion would transfer value from stayers rather than add it. Treasury shares repurchased are also transferable within 30 days of the period's end.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2% nominal, below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP, because the terminal business is a no-moat distributor of other people's digital products whose real volume has shrunk for four straight years; growth above inflation would require share gains we cannot source.

challenges.challenge: Valuation is 100% DCF, dropping the industry's 40% EV/sales leg; every published INTERNET_PLATFORMS peer (BELI, BUKA, EMTK, GOTO) carries both methods, and qc_justifications has no answer for weights.changed. The stated reason (multiples need profitable comparables) misstates EV/sales, which exists for loss-making platforms. The breakeven is EV/sales of 0.22x FY2026E revenue against the 0.55x the price implies.
challenges.answer: EV/sales retained as a cross-check with the breakeven stated: the peer median multiple is a platform margin, NFCX earns 4.8% gross, breakeven 0.22x against 0.55x implied. The weight change is now justified in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: The claim that terminal value is only 20.0% of EV, so the valuation is not a terminal-value artefact, hides the real dependency: FY2026E FCFF of Rp110.2bn is Rp141.7bn of working-capital release (delta_nwc), roughly Rp110bn of the Rp206.6bn EV after discounting; the 2027-30 releases add more. On the model's own rows and excluding the FY2026 release, EV is about Rp138bn.
challenges.answer: Rewritten: FY2026E FCFF of 55.0 is a 141.7 working-capital release, roughly a sixth of EV discounted; EV excluding FY2026 stated; TV share restated at 23.1%.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex is Rp105.0bn against Rp80.1bn already spent in H1, i.e. Rp25bn in H2 against an H1 run-rate near Rp160bn. The step-down is unsourced while inventory rose 45% and revenue fell 42% in the same half. Lower capex raises FCFF and EV, so this is an unjustified optimism in the base case, not conservatism.
challenges.answer: Capex FY2026E now 160.2, carrying H1 80.1 at twice its rate; the unsourced step-down is removed and the EV is lower on the higher capex.

challenges.challenge: The model sets tax to zero in all ten forecast years (pos(pbt) x 22%, PBT negative), yet the group paid Rp27.7bn of cash tax in H1-2026 alone against a pre-tax loss [S19] because profitable subsidiaries cannot offset loss-making ones. The base case omits a recurring ~Rp55bn/yr cash outflow, inflating FCFF and EV.
challenges.answer: Structural cash tax of 27.7 in H1 is now modelled as a claim: PV of ten years at the annualised rate deducted in the valuation bridge; the EV effect is stated.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A cash in the model is Rp191.5bn but the LK shows Rp145.8bn at 31 Dec 2025 [S19]; the Rp45.8bn gap is exactly 'Investasi lainnya', which the pack bundles into cash and the 30 June restatement strips out. So FY2026E cash of Rp283.7bn and net debt of -Rp39.3bn are not comparable with the Rp108.7bn cash and Rp342.6bn debt quoted elsewhere, and the 'net cash by year-end' statement is wrong by about Rp45bn.
challenges.answer: Cash restated to the LK basis for FY2024A and FY2025A; FY2026E cash 181.8 and net debt 62.6 now tie to the same basis and the net-cash claim is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The statement that trade receivables rose by roughly half against a falling top line [S25] is contradicted by the filing: third-party trade receivables fell from Rp222.6bn to Rp164.2bn (-26%) and related-party receivables rose only from Rp6.0bn to Rp10.5bn [S19]. The divergence flag is real for inventory (Rp216.0bn to Rp314.0bn), not for receivables.
challenges.answer: Receivables claim withdrawn: third-party receivables fell to 164.2 and related-party rose to 10.5; inventory 216.0 to 314.0 is now the sole divergence flag.

challenges.challenge: '109 of cash against 692 of financial liabilities' reads Rp691.9bn as debt. Note 37 shows 'Total Liabilitas Keuangan' is the amortised-cost category and includes trade payables, other payables, accrued expenses, customer deposits and taxes payable; debt-like instruments (convertibles 239.0, bank 84.3, financing 5.0, leases 14.3) total Rp342.6bn. Using 692 as a liability stack overstates leverage by roughly 2x and leans the risk section bearish beyond the evidence.
challenges.answer: Debt-like total restated to 342.6 (convertibles, bank, financing, leases); the 691.9 amortised-cost category is described as operating payables and removed from the risk framing.

challenges.challenge: The only asset that could clear the claims - 29.3% of DMMX at its Rp946bn market cap, Rp277bn or Rp418/share - is dismissed verbally (at market the minority claim is larger) without a number, and the market SOTP the report itself asks for is never computed. The bridge also adds associates (Rp101.5bn) but omits investment in shares Rp62.5bn, convertible bonds Rp40.0bn and other investments Rp31.5bn, Rp134bn in total.
challenges.answer: Bridge now credits 62.5 investment in shares, 40.0 convertible bonds and 31.5 other investments; SOTP at market stated with the minority marked at market and the per-share residual.

challenges.challenge: The board is buying up to 49mn shares at Rp1,775 - 98.6% of the price and 80% of group cash - while the report says the equity is worth zero. Either the board has information the model lacks or the buyback is a treasury trading operation (S15 shows 4.26mn treasury shares being re-sold). The report asserts value transfer but never addresses the signal.
challenges.answer: Buyback addressed as a signal: the prior programme re-sold all treasury shares via a broker over five months, so the board price is not information we can verify; the new size cannot be a trading operation at this ADTV.

challenges.challenge: The Rp239bn of ESB convertible notes carry a pending extension request - 'as of the issuance date ... the extension letter is still in process' [S19 p.100] - and the rate was raised to 12%. That is a concrete refinancing/default-type event, stronger and more dated than the generic 'if the bank lines are not renewed'.
challenges.answer: ESB convertible extension now the first liquidity risk and a dated catalyst, with the extension to 31 March 2026 and the 12% coupon stated.

challenges.challenge: The capital-allocation critique omits the price of the June-2025 private placement: 66.67mn shares, 10% of capital, at a nominal Rp100 per share [S12], 17.75x below the Rp1,775 buyback 17 months later. Issuing 10% at Rp100 and buying back 7.35% at Rp1,775 is the strongest related-party value-transfer datapoint in the file.
challenges.answer: S12 states a nominal value of Rp100 per share, not an issue price, and the FY2025 share count shows the placement did not execute; no price or subscriber is disclosed, so the 17.75x discount claim is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The rendered report carries 46 doubled-unit defects: '239 IDR bnbn', '442 IDR bnbn', '109 IDR bnbn', '49.0 mn sharesm', with every money figure in section 3 affected. The underlying numbers are right; the templates append a unit the fact already carries.
challenges.answer: All doubled-unit placeholders re-rendered on their native units, including every money figure in the financial section and the share counts.

challenges.challenge: FY2022 and FY2023 revenue (Rp9,836.6bn and Rp9,526.1bn), gross profit, opex and the -486.6/-128.7 non-operating charges are cited [S25], but S25 (FY2025 LK) contains none of them; they are in S24 (FY2023 LK), which shows Rp9,526.10bn and Rp9,836.62bn.
challenges.answer: FY2022 and FY2023 figures re-cited to S24, the FY2023 LK, which carries both years; the FY2025 LK citation is removed.

challenges.challenge: WACC 13.8% and COE 15.7% sit outside the house IDR band of 11-13% and above every peer but GOTO; terminal g of 2.0% is half the 4.0% all peers use. Both are argued and neither moves the rating (breakeven WACC 4.8%), but the card's output contract (band check, implied exit multiple vs entry) is not shown: implied exit EV/EBITDA is 2.1x against 19.5x entry.
challenges.answer: Band check and implied exit multiple added: terminal value is roughly twice terminal EBITDA against 21.8x entry, and the zero survives at the bottom of the band and at 4% growth.

challenges.challenge: The SELL is published as actionable on a name the packet marks uninvestable (ADTV Rp54mn, roughly 30k shares a day) and which cannot be shorted on IDX; the buyback alone equals about 1,600 days of ADTV. A -100% target on an untradeable line should be labelled as such rather than presented as a call the desk can execute.
challenges.answer: Execution constraint stated on the cover: ADTV of IDR54m, no shorting, buyback equal to years of turnover; SELL labelled as fundamental value, not an executable position.

challenges.challenge: Free float is given as 22.4% [S10, S17] but the S17 registrar table shows public 30.22%, treasury 0.64%, MCAS 51.29%, Inti DOT COM 11.65% and Bank of Singapore 6.04%; the konglo block sources 22.35% to S25, which has no free-float table. S14, the exchange unusual-market-activity note, is dated 14 March 2024 and is presented as a current governance signal.
challenges.answer: Free float now quoted from the August 2026 registrar table at 30.22% with the data-provider convention explained, and the exchange surveillance reference is dated March 2024.

missing_bull_case.note: The DMMX stake at market (29.3% x Rp946bn = Rp277bn = Rp418/share) is the one asset that could clear the claims and is dismissed without a number (C8); the bridge also omits Rp134bn of investment-in-shares, convertible bonds and other investments, though associates are added back. The board's own Rp1,775 buyback is treated only as value transfer, never as a valuation signal (C9).

missing_bear_case.note: The ESB convertible note extension was still in process at the LK date - a live refinancing event weaker than the report's generic bank-line caveat (C10). The June-2025 private placement price (nominal Rp100/share, 17.75x below the Rp1,775 buyback) is omitted, which is the strongest governance datapoint in the file (C11). Dollar-note FX sensitivity is qualitative only.

assumption_realism.note: Base case is generous, not cautious: FY2026E capex Rp105bn implies Rp25bn in H2 vs Rp80bn in H1 (C3); tax is zero in every forecast year against Rp27.7bn of H1-2026 cash tax (C4); the Rp141.7bn working-capital release is 66% of EV and depends on Rp314bn of inventory, up 45% in six months, converting at book (C2). Gross margin 4.8% vs 4.6% H1 and revenue +10% h/h in H2 are defensible.

evidence_and_citations.note: Trade receivables are claimed to have risen by half; the LK shows third-party receivables fell 26% from Rp222.6bn to Rp164.2bn (C6). 46 doubled-unit defects ('239 IDR bnbn', 'sharesm') across the rendered report (C12). FY2022/23 history is cited to S25 but sits in S24 (C13). The 692 liability figure is used as debt when note 37 shows it includes trade payables and accruals (C7).

valuation_method_fit.note: Method is 100% DCF, dropping the industry 40% EV/sales leg that every published peer carries, with no qc_justification (C1). The 'TV only 20%' defence ignores that ~Rp110bn of the Rp206.6bn EV is the FY2026 working-capital release (C2). The associates add-back is selective (C8). WACC 13.8% is outside the house 11-13% band and argued, and the breakeven WACC of 4.8% shows it does not drive the zero (C14). Bridge mechanics are otherwise sound.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose overstates leverage: '109 cash against 692 of financial liabilities' presents a note-37 category that includes trade payables, accruals, deposits and taxes as a debt stack, when debt-like instruments are Rp342.6bn (C7). A -100% SELL is published as actionable on a name the packet marks uninvestable (ADTV Rp54mn, ~30k shares/day) and cannot be shorted (C15).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Against five published INTERNET_PLATFORMS peers: every one blends DCF with EV/sales, WACC is 12.2-13.8% (NFCX at the top), terminal g is 4.0% for all (NFCX 2.0%). NFCX is the only shrinking revenue base, which justifies different drivers, but the method-weight difference is unexplained and the sector-relative breakeven is never shown (C1). FX from the house deck is used qualitatively only.

conservatism_audit.note: No unjustified conservatism that moves the rating. Below-peer items: WACC 13.8% vs 11-13% band, terminal g 2.0% vs 4.0% peers, revenue decline extended to FY2030, 30% liquidity discount on a zero. Each is argued and immaterial: breakeven WACC 4.8%, EV must rise 2.78x, and even at a 9% WACC EV is only Rp289bn against Rp574.8bn of claims. Scenario shocks are mirrored (+/-8pp growth, +/-1pp margin).

calibration.note: The BLOCK extreme_call is justified with sources and the calibration gap is 0.88pp (within tolerance). But the weights.changed WARN is unanswered, the model's FY2025A cash of Rp191.5bn does not tie to the LK's Rp145.8bn (Rp45.8bn of other investments bundled into pack cash), and FY2026E tax is zero against Rp27.7bn paid in H1 (C5, C4).

signoff.notes: TECHNOLOGY signoff, single-name batch; no sector tilt to test. SELL at the Rp0 limited-liability floor is defensible and the zero is a genuine claim-stack arithmetic result, not a single-input artefact: required EV = net debt 233.9 + NCI book 442.4 + PV structural cash tax 291.3 - associates 101.5 - investments 133.9 = 732.2 against modelled EV 176.6, i.e. 4.15x, and the report states the negative pre-floor equity per share rather than hiding it. Robustness checked: drop the whole 291.3 tax claim and required EV is still 440.8 (2.5x modelled); credit the 29.3% DMMX stake at its Rp946.2bn market value (277.2) instead of its DCF contribution and EV rises only to roughly the low 300s, still short even of the no-tax breakeven. The mean-reversion matcher and the EV/sales cross-check (0.22x breakeven vs ~0.55x implied) independently reject the price, and the 13.8% WACC/g 2.0% departures are argued with the 4.8% breakeven WACC stated. Carried to v2 with this note (none changes the sign, the rating or the target): (1) Q13 four customers above a tenth is wrong for two of four (Shopee 20.1%, Tokopedia 10.1%, Alfaria 8.1%, MCAS 7.5%); correct to two above a tenth, top four ~46%; (2) Q14 the 133.9 of added assets is under half the 277.2 DMMX stake at market, not about as much - the sentence overstates the credit, i.e. errs against the SELL; (3) Q15 stale 21.8x in the extreme_call justification - engine FY2025A is 21.14; (4) Q16 free float 22.4% in the section 3 WACC argument vs 30.22% registrar primary in section 6; (5) Q17 working capital releases IDR-151.9bn reads as a negative release; (6) Q18 the [S3, S4] citation cannot support a negative assertion of no enforcement action. Also for v2: reconcile the bull leg with section 4, which concedes a market-marked SOTP leaves a small fraction of the price (about Rp419/share, 23%) while the bull run returns 0 - all three scenarios return exactly 0 because the mirrored +/-8pp revenue and +/-1pp margin shocks cannot move EV from 176 to 732, so the probability weighting is non-binding and should be labelled as such. CONFIRMED: no deck or macro-variable overrides; calibration gap 0.59pp explained; konglo not applicable; the report already discloses ADTV Rp54m and no shorting, so the -100% is a fundamental-value statement, not an executable position.

bias.note: Base case is anchored to the last actual, not to caution: FY2026E revenue 2,459.1 is H1-2026 1,229.6 held at the run-rate [S19], gross margin 4.57% is the H1 actual, D&A restated to the LK 73.5/80.6, capex at 152.7 carries H1 at twice its rate rather than assuming a step-down, and opex is cut only to the H1 annualised level. The one unsourced-looking input, WACC 13.8% versus the 11-13% band, is argued and the zero survives at the band bottom and at 4% growth, so it does not drive the call. Scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers (+/-8pp revenue growth, +/-1pp gross margin) with base at 45%; the bear is larger than the bull on sourced customer and funding asymmetry. No unsourced conservatism or optimism moves the rating; SELL follows from EV 176.6 against claims of 732.1, not from a haircut stack.

recomputed.item: EV required before the parent retains anything

findings.finding: The claim that four customers each bought more than a tenth of FY2025 net revenue is repeated in sections 2, 5 and 6 and is wrong for two of the four: S25 p.130 shows Shopee 819.6 (20.1%), Tokopedia 411.3 (10.1%), Alfaria 331.0 (8.1%) and MCAS 304.1 (7.5%); only the first two cleared a tenth in FY2025 (Alfaria and MCAS cleared it in FY2024, which is why the note lists them). The combined 45.85% is right.

Section 4 says the three added bridge assets 'add about as much as the DMMX stake is worth at market'. They total 133.9 (62.5 + 40.0 + 31.5) against a DMMX stake of 277.2 (946.2 x 29.3%), i.e. under half, and the sentence reads as if the credits offset the only liquid asset in the structure.

The extreme_call justification still carries stale arithmetic in its parenthetical: '21.8x is the FY2025A multiple'. The engine's FY2025A EV/EBITDA is 21.14, because 21.8 was struck on the pre-restatement FY2025A EBITDA of 79.5 (5.96 EBIT + 73.5 D&A) that Q3 replaced with 82.0. Q6 asked for exactly this correction and it is only half done.
Q10 remains open: section 4 calls the free float 22.4% in the WACC argument while section 6 makes the registrar's 30.22% [F43] primary. The judge raised it again this round.

Q11 remains open: section 4 renders 'working capital releases IDR-151.9bn', embedding the sign inside the money label so a release reads as a negative release. The underlying delta_nwc of -151.9 is right and ties to FCFF 64.8 (EBIT -7.62 x 0.78 + 71.56 D&A - 152.71 capex + 151.91).

Q12 remains open: section 6 cites [S3, S4] for 'no index deletion or enforcement action is recorded' and S4 is a buyback news article that cannot support that negative; the section 2 competitive-positioning paragraphs still carry only the segment-note citation for the market-structure claims.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -4.1pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The step is sourced and one-directional: first-half 2026 alone spent Rp80.1bn on property and equipment against Rp45.8bn in the whole of FY2025, so FY2026 carries that half at roughly twice its rate on the smaller revenue base (Rp152.7bn, 6.2% of revenue); the ratio then reverts to the FY2024-25 norm because the build is a single hardware and Smart Commerce roll-out, not a recurring programme, and no multi-year capital plan is disclosed that would support holding 6% on a revenue base falling by forty per cent [S19, S25].

flags.message: expected return -100%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers put the equity at zero: (1) the consolidated enterprise value of Rp176.6bn from the DCF is smaller than the Rp239.0bn of dollar convertible notes plus the Rp442.4bn book value of non-controlling interests, and the claims would need an enterprise value of Rp732.1bn - four times the modelled one - before the parent retained anything [S19]; (2) operations consumed Rp49.4bn of cash in H1-2026 against Rp80.1bn of capex, funded from bank and related-party lines, leaving Rp108.7bn of cash [S19]; (3) a signage subsidiary only 29.30% owned is consolidated line by line, so three-fifths of consolidated equity belongs to minorities [S19]. Today's price of Rp1,800 implies 26.4x FY2026E EV/EBITDA (21.8x is the FY2025A multiple) on a shrinking, loss-making base, and the parent MCAS is capitalised at Rp162.3bn while consolidating NFCX at Rp1,192.3bn [S26, S10]. The floor at zero is limited liability, not a modelling artefact.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_sales': 0.4}
flags.justification: EV/sales stays a cross-check and not a weighted leg. The peer median of 0.73x is earned on platform gross margins of 15-30%, so applied to a 4.6% pass-through gross margin it implies about 16x gross profit and produces a positive equity value only by importing a different business model; the price itself already implies 0.49x FY2026E sales while the claims ranking ahead of the parent are cleared only at 0.30x, so the multiple is disclosed, bounded and not decisive [S19, S25]. The 40% leg is therefore replaced by the breakeven test rather than dropped.
